title: Articles: a / an / the / Ø
students_do: Students work out when to use a, an, the or nothing, then practise with targeted exercises.

data.text:
Articles: a / an / the / Ø
A2 / Grammar / 1:1 online / 30 min

Articles - the main trap for Slavic learners. The whole system in one lesson.

▸ Slavic speakers often omit articles completely at A1-A2
  ▸ Focus on a/the distinction first; zero article last
  ▸ "A university" vs "an hour" - test the SOUND rule
  ▸ Good drilling game: Article Rush (Tools → Grammar)

items.text: Understand when to use a, an, the, or nothing

data.title: 1. A / AN - indefinite (general / first mention)
data.desc:
A  → before consonant SOUND
       a book   a user   a university   a one-way street

  AN → before vowel SOUND
       an apple   an hour   an honest man   an MP

  Use for:
  • First mention:   I saw a dog.
  • Jobs/roles:      She's a teacher.
  • General:         A cat has four legs.

data.title: 2. THE - definite (specific, known to both)
data.desc:
Use when:
  • Mentioned before:  I saw a dog. The dog barked.
  • Only one exists:   the sun / the president / the Internet
  • Superlatives:      the best, the most expensive
  • Geography (rivers, oceans, mountain ranges):
    the Amazon, the Pacific, the Alps
  • Plural countries/groups:
    the USA, the Netherlands, the Beatles

data.title: 3. Ø - ZERO article (no article needed)
data.desc:
• Languages:       I speak English. (NOT the English)
  • Sports:          play football / tennis / chess
  • Meals:           have breakfast / lunch / dinner
  • Abstract nouns:  Love is beautiful. Time flies.
  • Proper names:    London, Ukraine, John
  • Plural generics: Dogs are loyal animals.

data.title: 4. EXAMPLES - complete the gap
data.desc:
1. She's ___ teacher at ___ local school.
     → a teacher / the local school

  2. Can you pass me ___ salt?
     → the salt (we both know which)

  3. I had ___ egg and ___ toast for breakfast.
     → an egg / Ø toast (uncountable)

  4. ___ Amazon is ___ longest river in ___ South America.
     → The Amazon / the longest / Ø South America

  5. He plays ___ guitar in ___ band.
     → Ø guitar / a band  (first mention)

title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
students_do: Students contrast Present Perfect with Past Simple and practise choosing between them.

data.text:
Present Perfect vs Past Simple
B1 / Grammar / 1:1 online / 45 min

The biggest confusion for Slavic speakers. A clear algorithm for choosing between tenses.

▸ SINCE vs FOR confusion is common - dedicate 5 min
  ▸ "For 3 years" can go with BOTH tenses - great discussion starter
  ▸ Game: Tense Picker (Tools → Grammar) works great here

items.text: Know when to use Present Perfect vs Past Simple
Identify key time signals for each tense
Avoid the #1 error for Slavic speakers

data.title: 1. THE RULE IN ONE LINE
data.desc:
Present Perfect = past action with PRESENT relevance
  Past Simple     = completed action in a FINISHED time

objectives.text: Know when to use Present Perfect vs Past Simple
Identify key time signals for each tense
Avoid the #1 error for Slavic speakers

data.notes:
Present Perfect = past action with PRESENT relevance
  Past Simple     = completed action in a FINISHED time

data.title: 2. PRESENT PERFECT (have/has + past participle)
data.desc:
Use for:
  ✓ Experience (ever/never):    Have you ever been to Japan?
  ✓ Recent news:                The president has resigned.
  ✓ Unfinished period (this week/today/this year):
                                I've sent 10 emails today.
  ✓ Result matters now:         I've lost my keys! (= I can't find them)
  ✓ With: already, yet, just, ever, never, so far, recently

  Time signals: today, this week, this year, ever, never,
                already, yet, just, recently, so far, since, for

data.title: 3. PAST SIMPLE (verb + -ed / irregular)
data.desc:
Use for:
  ✓ Specific finished time:     She left at 9 o'clock.
  ✓ Sequence of past events:    He arrived, sat down, and opened the file.
  ✓ Stories and narratives:     I lived in London for 3 years. (no longer)

  Time signals: yesterday, last week/month/year, in 2019,
                ago, when I was a child, at 5 pm, then

data.title: 4. COMPARISON TABLE
data.desc:
PP: I've been to Paris.         → I know it, connection to now
  PS: I went to Paris in 2019.    → specific finished trip

  PP: She's broken her leg.       → she can't walk NOW
  PS: She broke her leg in March. → past event, stated when

  PP: Have you eaten yet?         → today, result matters
  PS: Did you eat this morning?   → asking about specific time

title: Everyday Phrases & Idioms
students_do: Students learn everyday phrases and idioms and use them in short exchanges.

outline.name: MATCH THE IDIOM TO THE SITUATION

data.text:
Everyday Phrases & Idioms
B1 / Vocabulary / 1:1 online / 35 min

The top 25 colloquial phrases and idioms for natural English.

▸ Teach idioms in context - never in isolation lists alone
  ▸ Memory Match game: idiom ↔ meaning works perfectly here
  ▸ Ask students to find 3 idioms in articles - makes reading active

data.title: 1. TIME IDIOMS
data.desc:
in the nick of time     - exactly when needed, almost too late
  around the clock        - 24 hours a day, non-stop
  hit the ground running  - start something energetically
  the eleventh hour       - the last possible moment
  call it a day           - stop working/doing something for today
  buy time                - delay to get more time

title: Small Talk & Social English
students_do: Students practise opening, keeping up and closing a small-talk conversation.

data.text:
Small Talk & Social English
A2 / Speaking / 1:1 online / 30 min

The art of small talk: topics, phrases and cultural context.

▸ Hugely practical for professional and travel contexts
  ▸ Video clip: British vs American small talk on YouTube
  ▸ Debrief cultural differences - Slavic learners often find British
    indirectness confusing ("Not bad" = British compliment!)

items.text: Know what to talk about (and what to avoid!)

data.title: 1. SAFE SMALL TALK TOPICS (UK/US)
data.desc:
✓ Weather ("Beautiful day, isn't it?")
  ✓ Weekend plans ("Any plans for the weekend?")
  ✓ Work/studies (briefly - "How's work going?")
  ✓ Travel ("Have you been anywhere nice lately?")
  ✓ Food/restaurants ("Have you tried that new place on…?")
  ✓ Hobbies ("I've just got into hiking - do you…?")
  ✓ Sport (UK: football; US: baseball/American football)

  AVOID in small talk:
  ✗ Politics, religion, money, age, weight
  ✗ Very personal questions ("How much do you earn?")
  ✗ Controversial opinions with strangers

title: Discussion & Debate Language

data.text:
Discussion & Debate Language
B2 / Speaking / 1:1 online / 40 min

Language tools for discussions, debates and exchanging opinions.

▸ Assign positions randomly - great for pushing beyond comfort zone
  ▸ Give a language feedback sheet: note phrases students missed
  ▸ Use Four Opinions with a concrete class context to start the warm-up

data.title: 1. STATING YOUR OPINION

Neutral:      "I think / I believe / I feel that…"
  Strong:       "I'm convinced that… / I strongly believe…"
  Tentative:    "It seems to me that… / I tend to think…"
  Impersonal:   "It could be argued that… / One might say…"

Know the name:    Dear Mr Smith, / Dear Dr Kovač,
  Don't know name:  Dear Sir or Madam,
  Team:             Dear all, / Dear team,
  Informal formal:  Hi Sarah, (acceptable in many offices)

data.title: 4. OPENING SENTENCES
data.desc:
Introducing yourself:  "My name is [X] and I am writing with regard to…"
  Referring to contact:  "Further to our conversation on Monday…"
  Following up:          "I am writing to follow up on my previous email…"
  Requesting:            "I am writing to enquire about…"

BODY - keep it clear:
  One idea per paragraph. Use topic sentences.
  "Regarding the first point…"
  "I would like to draw your attention to…"
  "Please find attached…"
  "I would be grateful if you could…"

data.desc:
Requesting action:  "I look forward to hearing from you."
  Offering help:      "Please do not hesitate to contact me if you need further information."
  Thanking:           "Thank you for your time and consideration."

data.title: 6. SIGN-OFF
data.desc:
Formal:   Yours sincerely, (if you know the name)
            Yours faithfully, (if you don't know the name)
  Semi-formal: Kind regards, / Best regards,
  Informal formal: Best, / Many thanks,

data.title: 7. SAMPLE EMAIL
data.desc:
Subject: Application for English Teacher Position

  Dear Ms Thompson,

  I am writing to apply for the English Teacher position advertised
  on your school's website on 10 May. I believe my qualifications
  and experience make me a strong candidate for this role.

  I hold a CELTA qualification and have four years of experience
  teaching English to adult learners at B1-C1 level. In my current
  role at Language School Kyiv, I have developed a range of
  communicative lesson materials and achieved a 95% student
  satisfaction rate.

  Please find my CV attached. I would welcome the opportunity
  to discuss my application further at your convenience.

  I look forward to hearing from you.

data.title: 8. COMMON ERRORS
data.desc:
✗ "I am writing to you because I need to ask you…"  (too wordy)
  ✓  "I am writing to enquire about…"

  ✗ "With regards to your email…"
  ✓  "With regard to your email…" (no -s)

  ✗ "Waiting for your answer"
  ✓  "I look forward to your reply."
